# Plots in Cells {#chp:plots}

A table is good at exact numbers. A chart is good at patterns. Why not have both
in the same row? A forest plot of effect sizes is a table with a tiny chart in
one column. A before-and-after comparison is a table with a dot per visit. A
trend is a table with a little line running across it.

**lt** has three functions that draw these charts *inside cells*:
`lt_errorbar()` for intervals, `lt_dotplot()` for a few values per row, and
`lt_sparkline()` for a series of values per row. They are small, and they stay
small on purpose: each chart is a handful of SVG shapes, drawn by the browser
from the numbers in the table. No image is rendered, and no chart library is
loaded.

::: {.callout-tip data-legend="The lightweight promise"}
Only the numbers travel to the page. The shapes are drawn in the browser when the
table is shown. In an interactive table (@chp:interactive), that means only the
rows on the current page are drawn, so a sparkline on a page of 10 rows costs
10 drawings, not 10,000.
:::

## Error bars: a forest plot in a column {#sec:errorbar}

Confidence intervals are the classic case. Each row needs three numbers: the
estimate and its lower and upper bounds. Name them in a formula, estimate on the
left, bounds on the right, and **lt** draws the point and the bar on one shared
scale, so the rows are comparable at a glance:

```{r, child = ex('errorbar')}
```

The `ref = 0` argument draws a vertical line at zero, which is where you want a
reference line for a risk difference (or `ref = 1` for an odds ratio). The
`axis` argument draws a proper axis in the footer, with tick marks at round
values; pass a string to caption it, as above.

Look at the `into = "Forest"` argument. By default, the plot replaces the first
value column, which is tidy but hides the numbers. With `into`, the plot gets a
column of its own, and the numbers stay visible as text beside it. If the column
does not exist yet, **lt** creates it at the end, so use `lt_move()` (@sec:labels)
if you want it somewhere else.

### Several series in one cell

Sometimes one row should carry several intervals. Picture a trial with two
treatment arms, both compared with placebo: you want to see both differences for
each adverse event, and you want to see them on one scale. Give `lt_errorbar()`
one `estimate ~ lower + upper` formula per series. Each row then stacks one bar
per series, and `color` and `labels` explain which is which in a footer legend:

```{r}
d_grp = data.frame(
  Term = c("Headache", "Nausea", "Fatigue"),
  D1 = c(2.1, -1.4, 3.3), L1 = c(-1.0, -4.2, 0.1), U1 = c(5.2, 1.4, 6.5),
  D2 = c(-0.5, 0.8, 1.2), L2 = c(-3.6, -2.1, -1.9), U2 = c(2.6, 3.7, 4.3)
)
lt(d_grp) |>
  lt_errorbar(
    D1 ~ L1 + U1, D2 ~ L2 + U2, ref = 0, color = TRUE,
    labels = c("Drug A", "Drug B"), axis = "Risk difference (%)"
  )
```

`color = TRUE` takes colors from the current palette. Pass a character vector
such as `c("#5b8ff9", "#f6903d")` if you want specific ones. The bounds are
hidden by default because the plot already shows them. `color = FALSE`, the
default, draws every series in a single color, and the legend is then omitted.

::: {.callout-tip data-legend="Scale"}
Every bar in a column shares one scale. The scale runs from the smallest to the
largest finite value across all the columns the plot reads, so a single extreme
row squeezes the rest. Set `limits = c(min, max)` to choose the scale yourself,
for example to match another table, or to keep a confidence interval that runs
off the chart from being clipped unnoticed. Values outside the limits are pinned
to the edges.
:::

## Dot plots: a few values per row {#sec:dotplot}

A dot plot answers a different question. Instead of an interval, each row has a
handful of measurements, and you want to see where each one lands. Before and
after is the everyday example: one dot for each visit, all on the same axis, so
the movement is obvious even before you read the numbers.

```{r, child = ex('dotplot')}
```

Give `lt_dotplot()` the value columns as a formula, one dot per column. The
`color = TRUE` argument colors the dots from the palette and adds a legend, and
`axis` (on by default) puts the shared axis in the footer. The title of the
axis is the string you pass, here `"Score"`.

Two dots that land on nearly the same value sit on top of each other, and one of
them vanishes. That is what `stagger = TRUE` is for, as in the example above: it
moves each column's dot onto its own track, so both stay visible. The position
up or down is cosmetic. The value still reads from left to right, and the cell
grows taller to make room for the tracks.

::: {.callout-warning data-legend="Labels"}
The cell shows every column at once, so its column header should name them all.
Use `lt_label()` to write something like `"Before / After"`, as the example
does. Otherwise a reader sees a single "Before" header over a row of dots that
mean two things.
:::

## Sparklines: a trend in a cell {#sec:sparkline}

A sparkline is a word-sized line chart. Edward Tufte popularized the idea of
putting such graphics inside a sentence, and it works just as well inside a table row. You
can give `lt_sparkline()` a series in two ways. The first is a **list-column**,
where each cell holds a vector of numbers:

```{r, child = ex('sparkline')}
```

Each row is scaled to its own range by default, so the shape is what you see, and
the actual values are in the cells next to it. The `type = "bar"` argument draws
bars instead of a line, and `color` sets the color of either.

The second way is to spread the series over several ordinary columns, one per
point, read left to right across each row. This is handier when your data are
already wide, as in a quarterly report:

```{r}
d_q = data.frame(
  Region = c("North", "South", "West"),
  Q1 = c(2, 5, 4), Q2 = c(4, 3, 6), Q3 = c(6, 7, 5), Q4 = c(5, 2, 8)
)
lt(d_q) |>
  lt_label(Q1 = "Quarterly sales") |>
  lt_sparkline(~ Q1 + Q2 + Q3 + Q4, type = "bar", limits = c(0, 8), color = "#4caf50")
```

Here the four quarter columns are hidden after the first, since their values now
live in the chart. Use `hide = FALSE` to keep them visible.

### A shared scale for honest comparisons

Per-row scaling makes every line fill its cell, which is pretty but can mislead.
A row that moves from 2 to 3 looks just as dramatic as one that goes from 20 to
30. When the rows should be compared with each other, pass `limits` to put every
sparkline on one scale. The example above did exactly that with `limits = c(0,
8)`, so the North and West rows can be read against each other directly.

## Sizing and layout {#sec:plot-size}

Each plot is a fixed pixel size by default: `width` and `height` set it, and
`width = 160` for `lt_errorbar()` is a sensible start. If you want the plot to
follow its column, give a relative width such as `"100%"`. The plot then grows and
shrinks as the column is resized, which pairs nicely with the resizable columns
of an interactive table (@chp:interactive). Use `list(min = 200, width = "100%")` to
keep it from shrinking below 200 pixels.

::: {.callout-tip data-legend="Interactive tables"}
Plots work in interactive tables, and they are drawn only for the visible page.
Sorting a table with a sparkline in it reorders the rows and redraws their
charts. Filtering keeps the charts of the rows that remain.
:::

## Where the charts live {#sec:plot-module}

Inline plots come from their own module, `lt-plot.js`, which is loaded only for
tables that use one. A plain table does not pay for it. `lt_dependency(plot =
TRUE)` (@chp:js) includes it explicitly when you embed a table elsewhere, and
**lt** handles it for you everywhere else.
